newsitem.title: USA: Great Western in pact to be acquired by Washington Mutual.
newsitem.headline: Great Western in pact to be acquired by Washington Mutual.

text.p: Washington Mutual Savings Bank said Thursday it agreed to buy Great Western Financial for $6.6 billion, topping a rival offer from H.F. Ahmanson and Co. and opening a bidding war for the California thrift.
The deal, which would create the nation's largest savings and loan with $87.4 billion in assets, exceeds the $6.1 billion bid made last month by Ahmanson, currently the biggest thrift.
The merged Washington Mutual-Great Western would have about 1,500 offices and branches in the West and in Florida after closing 200 overlapping branches, mostly in California.
Washington Mutual was widely expected to bid for Great Western, which had been seeking a better deal since Ahmanson announced its bid on Feb. 18.
Ahmanson criticised the Great Western-Washington Mutual deal, and analysts and takeover specialists said the thrift was likely to raise its bid for Great Western.
"It's unlikely that their first bid would be their last bid," said Steven Cohen, research director at Kellner, DiLeo and Co., a money management firm.
Ahmanson said it would pursue legal action to require Great Western to treat all offers equally and to challenge its $195 million lock-up fee with Washington Mutual.
Ahmanson said it was confident investors would prefer its proposal and that it planned to hold an investment community meeting March 10 in New York to discuss its bid.
An Ahmanson spokesman said the company was "fully committed to a proposed transaction with Great Western," and criticised Washington Mutual's predicted cost savings from the deal.

Some analysts agreed. "I don't think this deal is as good as what people think. When you look to cut expenses and grow revenues simultaneously, its a tough hurdle," said Thomas Theurkauf, analyst with Keefe Bruyette Woods.
Washington Mutual Savings Bank Chief Executive Kerry Killinger said the proposed acquisition would boost earnings 5 percent in 1998 and 11 percent in 1999.

Great Western and Washington Mutual expect cost savings of $208 million in 1998 and $340 million in 1999 from branch closings and other consolidation. Ahmanson said its proposed merger with Great Western would save $400 million a year.
Some observers have said Ahmanson made a tactical error when it said job cuts would come mostly from Great Western. Analysts estimated job losses in the Ahmanson proposal would total about 2,500.

Great Western Chief Executive John Maher said cost cuts in a merger with Washington Mutual would be distributed evenly and that job losses would be much less than in a merger with Ahmanson. He did not elaborate.
Maher said there was no comparison between the Great Western and Ahmanson proposals.
"We have a definitive agreement with very clear-cut terms and we think it is in the best interest of shareholders. It's onward and upward and we have every intention of closing the deal," he said.
But many in the industry said the fight was far from over.
"This is boiling down to a battle of two giants and seeing who has the iron stomach," said Lloyd Greif, president of Greif and Co., an investment banking firm.
"Right now, it appears Washington Mutual has the edge and Ahmanson is going to have to significantly raise its bid."

Great Western stock jumped $1.875 to $46.875 on the New York Stock Exchange, indicating investors believe the bidding may not be over. Washington Mutual shares fell 25 cents $53 on Nasdaq, while Ahmanson fell $1.25 to $40.75 on the NYSE.
Under the deal, Great Western shareholders would receive 0.9 share of Washington mutual for each Great Western shares.
Ahmanson's offer to exchange 1.05 of its shares for each Great Western share was originally valued at $6.5 billion but has slipped because Ahmanson stock has fallen.
Washington Mutual had been discussing a possible rival bid since last month. The Seattle-based thrift has been making acquisitions and said it would like to expand in California.

Its $1.6 billion acquisition of California-based American Savings last year from a company affiliated with Texas investor Robert Bass gave it a toehold in California, where thrifts are merging rapidly, and makes it a compelling fit with Great Western.
Great Western and Washington Mutual said the merger would rank Washington Mutual third in California. Great Western, based in Chatsworth, Calif., also has operations in Florida.

On a conference call, Killinger said he contacted Great Western shortly after he heard about Ahmanson's bid. Killinger would serve as chief executive of the merged company while Maher would continue as a director.

Some observers believe Washington Mutual is poised to win. "The leg-up in a situation like this is normally with the friendly bidder," said Cohen. "They've bid higher and have the blessing of the board."

Analysts have said Ahmanson, based in the Los Angeles suburb of Irwindale, could become a takeover target itself if it fails in its bid for Great Western. Great Western is based in Chatsworth in southern California.
